title: Re-evaluation of lecithins (E 322) as a food additive
authors: EFSA Panel on Food Additives and Nutrient Sources added to Food (ANS), Mortensen A, Aguilar F, Crebelli R, Di Domenico A, Frutos MJ, et al.
funder: European Food Safety Authority; requestor: European Commission.
result: Phosphatidylcholine is absorbed intact or as lysophosphatidylcholine or choline after intestinal hydrolysis; dietary lecithins are hydrolysed by phospholipases to liberate choline. No need for a numerical ADI and no safety concern at reported uses, including for choline from lecithins. Lecithins (E 322) are used as emulsifying and stabilising agents of water-oil/fat mixtures in a wide range of foods. Identity: lecithins (E 322) are mixtures or fractions of phosphatides obtained by physical procedures from animal or vegetable foodstuffs, including hydrolysed products; JECFA treats lecithin (INS 322i) and partially hydrolysed lecithin (INS 322ii) as separate additives with distinct specifications; the main source is soya bean oil, with cottonseed, maize, sunflower, rapeseed and egg yolk of minor importance; JECFA set no numerical ADI (ADI 'not limited') in 1974. Food-grade lecithin from soya or other sources contains about 60% phospholipids and 40% triglycerides, sterols and carbohydrates; the phospholipid composition of soya bean lecithin on an oil-free basis is 21% phosphatidylcholine, 22% phosphatidylethanolamine, 19% phosphatidylinositol, 10% phosphatidic acid, 1% phosphatidylserine and 12% glycolipids, while 31P-NMR data from the European Lecithin Manufacturers Association give 12.69 to 22.23% phosphatidylcholine for liquid and de-oiled soya lecithin. Choline that can theoretically be released is 13.2% for phosphatidylcholine with two linoleate groups and up to 3.38% for commercial lecithins. Authorisation: Group I additive at quantum satis in most food categories, among them cocoa and chocolate products, bread and rolls, and fine bakery wares; 30,000 mg/kg in fats and oils essentially free from water; 1,000 mg/L in infant and follow-on formulae and in the corresponding foods for special medical purposes; 10,000 mg/kg in processed cereal-based and baby foods and other foods for young children. Bread and rolls and fine bakery wares were the largest contributors to exposure in most surveys for all groups above infancy, and formulae in infants. Refined brand-loyal mean exposure ranged from 7 mg/kg body weight per day in adolescents to 82 mg/kg bw per day in children, with 95th percentiles of 15 to 187; dietary lecithin from the regular diet is about 1 to 5 g/day, 14 to 71 mg/kg bw per day for a 70 kg adult. On trimethylamine, the Panel states that high doses of choline cause a fishy body odour through excretion of trimethylamine formed by bacterial action, but that lecithin does not present that risk because intestinal bacteria in general cannot cleave the esters and hence do not form major amounts of trimethylamine from choline, citing Zeisel et al. (1983) as cited in IOM (1998). Toxicology: no concern for genotoxicity; no adverse effects in chronic or carcinogenicity studies in rats up to 3,750 mg/kg bw per day; no reproductive toxicity study available; indications of altered brain development at 5% soya lecithin and above in the diet during gestation, lactation and post-weaning, in studies of limited relevance, for which a study to OECD TG 426 was recommended. The opinion does not assess trimethylamine N-oxide and cites no study of lecithins with cardiovascular outcomes.
